plants.name: Helianthus annuus
plants.description: Tall, sturdy stalks carry dinner-plate-sized flower heads. Golden-orange rays frame a dark brown to purplish center, and the whole crown follows the sun across the sky. Fields of them glow across the American Midwest in late summer.
plants.bloomingSeason: July to October, peaking in late summer
plants.location: Central United States (Kansas and Missouri) and the wider North American prairie region
plants.funFact: What looks like one big flower is really hundreds of tiny florets packed into a head, and the florets in the center spiral in a pattern linked to the Fibonacci sequence.

plants.name: Chamerion angustifolium (Epilobium angustifolium)
plants.description: Spires of rosy-magenta blossoms rise up to two metres tall and light up burned clearings, roadsides and tundra edges. Flowers open from the bottom of the spike upward through the summer.
plants.bloomingSeason: July to September, with peak bloom in late July and early August in Alaska
plants.location: Alaska and other northern boreal regions of North America
plants.funFact: Alaskans say summer is nearly over once the topmost flower on the spike opens. The plant gets its name from how fast it colonizes land after wildfires.

plants.name: Dimorphotheca sinuata
plants.description: In the Southern Hemisphere's late winter, South Africa's semi-desert turns into a carpet of glowing orange daisies. Their petals open to follow the sunshine, and mix with vygies and spring bulbs to cover whole valleys.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late winter to spring, from August to mid-October, with the best displays from mid-August
plants.location: Namaqualand and the West Coast of South Africa, including Kirstenbosch National Botanical Garden in Cape Town
plants.funFact: The flowers close on cloudy days and at night, so the show is best on sunny afternoons. The seeds can lie dormant in the dry soil for years until good rains arrive.
